notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0057.tlg050.1st1K-gr: In 2.1 the parenthetical (ἐστὶν) of the edition is left untranslated as sense-redundant. 'τοῦ περιτοναίον ῥαγέντος ἢ ἀνευρυνθέντες' appears corrupt (case mismatch, and the sense 'remind them of the peritoneum burst...' is strained); translated as nearly as the text allows. The sentence 'οὐκ ἄν τις ὀρθῶς φαίη φαύλως μὲν διακεῖσθαι, εἶναι δὲ αὐτῇ τὸ βαρῦνον πολὺ' is logically awkward; perhaps a negative has dropped out (sense would be that one cannot say it is badly affected yet that what weighs on it is not much). 'ἀναλογισμῷ' rendered 'analogical reasoning'.

Line 3.1: the bracketed '(εἰς τὸ πάσχον)' after 'from what acts' appears to be a dittography in the edition and is not translated twice. 'ἔγχυμα' rendered 'contents (enchyma)': the term for fullness measured by the containing space. Line 4.1: 'καὶ τάχα ἄν τις ἐν τούτοις τοῖς σπλάγχνοις ᾖ' is evidently corrupt; read as 'εἴ τις' ('if there is any'). 'παρ έγχυμα' read as παρέγχυμα (parenchyma). Philippus is not securely identified (probably the pneumatist/empiric physician mentioned elsewhere by Galen).

First passage: 'ὑπὸ γὰρ (τῆς) τῶν μυῶν (ἐν) ὅλου κώλου κινουμένου' is corrupt in the edition; translated by the evident sense. 'ἕτοιμεν' read as ἕτοιμον. In 'σκέψεως ἑτέρας ... ᾖ' the verb appears corrupt; rendered as 'is'. 'Parenthetical conjunctions' (παραδιαζευκτικῶς) refers to the Stoic logical distinction between exclusive and non-exclusive disjunction. Second passage: 'ἑλκώδεις' refers to the 'ulcerous' type of lassitude (ἑλκώδης κόπος).

Line 7.1: 'ὀλίγον εἶναι' is odd; rendered 'in a short time' (perhaps read ὀλίγου χρόνου or similar). The bracketed '(μόρια)' in 8.1 appears to be an intrusive word or marginal note and is left untranslated. '(περιεχομένων)' is kept as the edition prints it. '(ἡ διὰ χρόνον σημείωσις τοῦ πλήθους)' looks like a marginal heading that has slipped into the text. 'καίτοι γε ὧν ὡς … οὐ κακῶ' is corrupt; translated as if reading 'καίτοι γε τοῖς … οὐ κακῶς'. The following clause ('ἔτι γε μὴν μᾶλλον, ὡς …') is also syntactically difficult, and the rendering is tentative. Works cited: the second book of The Causes of Symptoms, the fourth of On Matters of Health (De sanitate tuenda), On the Faculty of Drugs, and On Mixtures.

In 9.1 'recollection' (ἀνάμνησις) is the Empiricist technical term for the remembered indication. In 10.1 'κοινὸν κοινὸν' is a printing duplication, translated once. The clause 'ὅ ποτε ὁμωνυμίαις ἐνδείκνυται' appears corrupt; rendered tentatively. The sentence beginning 'For the most part, then, the fat increases in proportion' is obscure as transmitted; rendered literally. 'λογικοί' (Rationalists) is taken as equivalent to the Dogmatists.

Line 1: '(διὰ)' is an editorial supplement; the sense is the same either way. The final clause 'neither of these being seen in the fullness relative to the faculty' is compressed and its construction is uncertain. Line 2: the conditional 'if [it arises] through some external cause…' has no main clause in the Greek (anacoluthon); the sense is that redness so caused is not a sign of fullness. 'They do not let the arteries share in blood' refers to the view of Nicarchus and Praxagoras that the arteries do not contain blood.

The parenthesis 'μελαγχολικὸς χυμὸς ἕως οὗ λέγεται' is awkward and may be an intruded gloss; translated as it stands. Read θερμαινομένης for θερμαινομένη. In 'ἐπὶ τούτοις ἅπασι ... προσθεὶς' the participle lacks a main verb; '[one should judge]' supplied.

nodes.text: You will hardly find a word that nearly all present-day doctors use more often than 'fullness', or one they understand less. Of those among them who can give and take an account, most answer anyone who asks what they mean by fullness that the word is used relatively, like 'much' and 'little', so that it cannot be confined within a measure: what is much for one is sometimes less for another. And when you question them further and ask them to state the thing relative to which they say fullness exists, some become more silent than fish, while others babble at such length and so strangely that one cannot follow what they say. A very few answer that 'much' and 'little' are understood relative to the faculty. If you then ask them in turn what they mean by faculty, some do not answer at all; of those who venture to state something, no one says the same as anyone else, and most explain anything rather than faculty. And if one of them should be found sensible enough to say that the faculty is either an active substance or an active cause, and he is then asked, first, whether there is any such substance governing the animal, and then, if there is, to explain what exactly it is, even he no longer answers the question put to him, but either falls completely silent or carries the argument off into something such that it would be better to keep silent. And if even among these someone should be found so prudent as to say that he cannot tell what the substance of the faculty is, but infers that it exists from its works, then again, when this man in his turn is asked whether he has examined and refuted what Asclepiades and many Asclepiadeans and Methodists have written to show that there is no faculty at all in animals, he appears not even to know whether they said it. As for those who say the faculty does not exist, it is rather obvious that they deny that fullness is understood and constituted relative to it, since it is impossible for fullness to be constituted and understood relative to a thing that does not exist at all. They suppose that 'much' and 'little' exist only relative to the capacity of the vessels; and sometimes they do not even use the term fullness at all, nor take from it any indication for evacuation, but only from constriction, which, as has been shown elsewhere, none of them explains in the same way. There is also a third band, which neither knows whether or not there is any faculty nor admits to inquiring into it, but claims to have found evacuation by long experience in the case of certain clearly apparent signs arising in the patient. Then, asked what these signs are, they say: distension of the vessels, redness and heaviness of the whole body, sluggishness toward movement, and tension of the limbs. Some of them also add the ulcerous and the fatigued sensation, and an idle previous life with rather large intake of food and drink, and the suppression of the customary excretions. With this concurrence (for that is what they call the combination of symptoms) they say venesection has been observed to help. These men, then, deprive not only themselves but all other people too of reason, claiming that everything was found by experience. The others, as was just said, claim to use reason, and of these some say that the faculty does not exist at all, others that it exists but that its substance is not known; so that very few venture to declare both the existence and the substance of the faculty. But even these do not all declare the same number or the same substance; indeed, of those who have left us writings, some, rather carelessly, always speak as if of a single faculty governing the animal, without adding any reasoning, while others attempt a demonstration and say there is not more than one. So it follows necessarily that whoever declares that there is fullness in the patient's body has already departed both from the so-called Empiricist doctors and from the Methodists, and speaks of 'much' either relative to the faculty or relative to the vessels.

So let our argument against the Empiricists and Methodists be put off, and let us proceed to the others, who say they practise the art with reasoning. And yet some of today's men have come to such a pitch of audacity that they ascribe to themselves the names of a sect, yet know nothing even of those [sects'] own [doctrines]. One can often hear many of them saying at the bedside of the sick that the man is full and must be bled, and then again, when the discussion comes up, calling themselves Methodists or Empiricists. But, as I was saying, having come to those who use analogical reasoning, let us first converse with those among them who always understand 'much' relative to the faculty. For these men seem never to have seen wineskins or sacks filled beyond measure, nor ever to have taken more food than they should, so as to distend the stomach, nor ever to have collected urine in the bladder beyond what is proper, or faeces in the rectum. For in all such circumstances each of the organs mentioned is visibly distended, so that the person is distressed unless he soon excretes the excess. Nor indeed is the sensation the same as that of something weighing down, or biting, or causing distress by some indescribable quality. One can indeed hear even laymen describing clearly what happens to them, without the contentiousness about doctrine: sometimes as being weighed down and oppressed by food, even though they have taken very little; sometimes as if they were bitten and eaten away; and often, being unable to describe exactly what happens, they say they feel nauseous. For none of these sensations is the same in people as that which arises when the stomach is stretched and distended to the utmost by an immoderate quantity of food. In such conditions they say their belly is in danger of bursting, while we too see it stretched to the utmost; but where they say they are weighed down, we sometimes see the stomach contracted. So too with the bladder: one condition is that in which it holds a very great amount of fluid, another when it holds little, or is weighed down. And accordingly one can see that the excretion is very copious in the bladder stretched because it has been filled, but in the one weighed down very scanty yet very frequent; for it does not wait for the time it takes to fill, but longs to throw off the distressing thing at once, just as when it is bitten by its quality. For then too it makes the excretion continuous. And indeed, when it is weighed down as if by a load of what it contains, one could not rightly say that it is in a bad state and yet that what weighs on it is much, even if it does not distend its coat at all. If the leaders of this opinion say anything at all against these things, while those who hold the contrary deny it, we must ask both again whether the bladder suffers the same distress when it is stretched in every direction and in danger of bursting, because it can no longer contain its contents, as when it is weighed down and bitten. For here again those who always understand fullness relative to the capacity of the vessels readily agree; but those who [understand it] relative to the faculty are vexed at such questions and grow angry, resisting in all sorts of ways, up and down, because they do not want to concede that this too is fullness. We, then, praying that both would stop their contentiousness, have urged them to agreement: those who think fullness is never spoken of relative to the space of what contains it (with whom we began our discussion first), urging them to yield to the truth, recalling that filled parts suffer distress in being distended; and those who think fullness arises only in this way, [urging them] to concede that what weighs down is much for what is weighed down. Again, shaming each party by what is clearly apparent, let us remind in particular those who say 'much' is understood only relative to the faculty of the peritoneum burst or widened by a quantity of food, and point out to them among external things wineskins and bladders suffering this, and sometimes even the jars themselves, when the fullness is of violent air. And let us ask about those who have coughed up blood from the lung through the rupture of a vessel, without a blow or a fall or any other such violence from outside, whether they do not think these too suffered thus from a very great fullness distending the vessel. And again let us remind the others in particular that a young man in good condition and a very small child cannot carry the same weight; for what is, I suppose, heaviest for the child is lightest for the young man. Shall we then say that what someone cannot carry is not a load at all, nor what weighs on him in this way much? Or shall we call it a load and heavy, but not allow it to be called fullness? But in that case the dispute will be not about a thing but about a word. And on the other alternative, you would not even think him a human being who says that he never feels weighed down at all, not even if you put twenty talents on his shoulder. But against those who have subjected themselves to a slavish doctrine nothing is sufficient. So now let us leave these men, or rather, if the truth must be told, bid them be gone, and converse with whoever is free and a friend of truth.

For we laid down two notions and relations of fullness: one relative to the strength and faculty of what carries it, the other relative to the space that receives it. And having laid these down, let us consider how many faculties of the animal there are in all, and how we shall either recognise or treat the fullness relative to each of them; and in addition to these, how many kinds in all there are of the fluids themselves, whether of those that weigh down the faculty, or of those that are not contained in the vessels. For it is in these matters that the doctor must be industrious and great, not in despising what is evident, which is the starting point of all demonstration. But perhaps it is no wonder that this very thing is unknown to those who have not examined anything about demonstration, and have neither discovered, nor learned, nor practised it. At any rate they are so simple-minded that even now someone who reads this writing expects, first, that I shall demonstrate in this treatise what anyone must certainly know who intends to examine anything about fullness accurately, and second, that I shall find the diagnosis and treatment of each kind of fullness; not realising that if things so great were by nature capable of being demonstrated in a single book, the art would not be long. I, however, have demonstrated in my work On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato that the faculty in the arteries is different from that in the nerves and veins. And in the same treatise I taught also that the heart is a kind of source of the faculty of the arteries, the brain of that of the nerves, and the liver of that of the veins. And in the work On the Elements according to Hippocrates I demonstrated that the substance underlying coming-to-be and passing-away is altered through the whole of itself according to the four qualities, moistness and dryness, heat and cold, and that the proper substance of each body lies in a particular blending of these, and that for this reason the peculiarity of the blending is also the substance of the faculties that govern them. This has also been shown by me in the work On the Natural Faculties, and separately in another treatise. Diagnostic signs have also been stated many times already in many treatises, both of each of the two kinds of fullness, and separately of each of the [varieties] within each. By 'each of the two' I mean the one relative to the faculty and the one relative to the contents (*enchyma*); for that is what they call the other kind of fullness, which is measured by the containing space, and which arises not only in animals but no less in inanimate things too: in woven cloths and plaited work, and in skins, and in vessels of earthenware, bronze and iron, and in those made of bronze, silver and tin. For these too burst when a large amount of airy substance is shut up in them, unless someone should wish that even such fullness arises relative to the cohesive faculty, forgetting the notion we mentioned at the beginning in connection with the word 'faculty', when we said that it is an active cause, as it makes no difference whether one says 'active' or 'productive'. Nor do we object if someone wishes to say that the faculty is a substance and not a productive cause; we wish only that this be preserved in the discussion, that the faculty is called active and productive, and is not a passive and material cause or substance. For if this is preserved, it is clear that the faculty will be the cause of some activity; and the activity itself must surely be a motion from what acts into what is acted on, just as the affection is the motion in what is acted on from what acts; so that the conception of the faculty lies in the category of relation, and its existence in its relation to something else. But to say that anything acts on itself, or is active upon itself, is contrary to the notion; and so too [to say that anything] holds itself together. For indeed those who most of all introduced the cohesive faculty, such as the Stoics, make what holds together one thing and what is held together another: the airy substance is what holds together, the material substance what is held together; whence they say that air and fire hold together, while earth and water are held together. Yet some of those who nowadays call themselves Herophileans, without having heard of these things even in a dream, make bold pronouncements about the cohesive faculty: they admit they do not know whether air, or fire, or both together is what holds together stones and pieces of wood and all other such things, but they declare simply that there is some faculty that holds all such things together, since they would dissolve and flow apart if nothing drew them together and bound them tight. Then, asked whether they venture to use in their reasoning such an axiom as that all existing things need something to hold them together, or not, they at once readily pronounce on the question and affirm it; but when led from there to an absurdity, they retract what they said and grow angry with the questioners as meddlesome and sophists. For this, if anything, is what the doctors of today have practised: to pronounce readily on the greatest doctrines, and, when refuted, to be annoyed and call those who refute them sophists. How then the argument is necessarily led into an absurdity once we posit that everything that exists needs a cohesive cause, I shall now go through for you. The cohesive cause, whatever it is (for the Herophileans do not claim to know it): do they themselves suppose it to be one of the things that exist, or of those that do not? If it is one of the things that do not exist, I marvel at the wisdom of these men, if they say that each existing thing needs something that does not exist. But if they place the cohesive cause among existing things, let them remember that they said everything that exists needs a cohesive cause in order to exist. For so it will follow that the cause itself needs another cause in order to exist, and that one in turn another, and so on to infinity. And if they say that of existing things some need another cause in order to exist, while others have their existence from themselves, first let them know that they no longer keep the original axiom, which they said was true above all else, that everything that exists needs a cohesive cause in order to exist; and second, that they need a very long argument [to show] why some need it and others do not, or indeed which things of these are of each sort. For neither most of the Herophileans nor the more recent Stoics state any demonstration that breath and fire hold together both themselves and other things, while water and earth need something else to hold them together. For as far as first appearances go, what is hard, resistant and dense might be said to hold itself together, while what is rare, soft and yielding [might be said] to need something else to hold it together. Not only do these men, without stating any demonstration, expect their hypothesis to be believed, but they no longer even notice that they are positing one that conflicts with itself. For the things that are the finest in their parts, the softest and most yielding of all, fire and air, these they say are the cause of the hardness and resistance of earth, as though it were possible for one thing to impart to another a faculty, nature, activity or quality in which it does not itself share. And indeed it is plainly seen that not only is nothing held together by fire, but everything is dissolved by it. Against the hypothesis of the Stoics, then, I have spoken at greater length elsewhere; I return to the Herophileans, and against them it will be enough for me for the present to say that their leader has fallen into the most contradictory position: he is at a loss in very many matters that have ready demonstrations, while he makes pronouncements in others whose demonstrations are impossible and whose hypothesis is false.

Leaving these men too, then, let us say again that being distended and bursting through fullness is an affection of the containing vessels themselves, not of any faculty; while being weighed down is [an affection] of the sensitive faculty. And not even this belongs to that faculty in every case simply; at any rate being weighed down is not an affection of the natural faculty. If, then, we rightly demonstrated in the treatise On the Natural Faculties that there is one faculty that attracts what is proper [to a part], another that alters these same things, another that retains them, and a fourth that separates out what is foreign, we must look for certain other indications of fullness relative to each of the faculties mentioned, since weight is not sufficient. For the vein and the artery do not perceive what weighs on them in the way that a weak stomach perceives it, through its excess of sensation; they have not the same sensation but another, if indeed it is not the same in kind as that in the nerves, a matter that would need a longer discussion to explain and establish. Now for fullness in the arteries relative to their faculty, scientific indications have been given in the treatise on the pulse; but those who glibly name fullness every day know none of these either. For fullness relative to the veins, however, I have neither discovered any scientific sign myself nor been able to find one written down by anyone else, seeing that no one before us has distinguished scientifically even the faculties themselves to begin with. The followers of Philippus and Archigenes touched on the theory of them a little, but none of them worked it out completely. The present discussion, however, seeks not only these things but also the fullness in each part, such as in the liver, or heart, or kidneys, or colon, or brain, or bone. Those of them, then, that are either barely sensitive or insensitive would not perceive the superfluities in them in the same way as the stomach and bladder do, but some not at all, and others either very faintly or not at all: very faintly with a very great fullness, not at all with a small one. For indeed a sensation of weight sometimes arises in the lung, the liver and the kidneys, and someone has felt a bone being weighed down, he too with a faint sensation; and in the brain weights often make themselves known that are not only faint but sometimes even very distinct. But in insensitive parts no sensation can arise, either of weight or of any other symptom; and some of the bones seem to be insensitive, and the fat, and some of the glands, unless indeed all the marrows too are among the insensitive things; at any rate the brain and spinal marrow, as some say, are among the sensitive. One could declare with confidence regarding the flesh at the convex part of the liver, which most doctors call parenchyma, for no nerve at all grows into it from anywhere; and one might be in doubt also about [the flesh] in the concave part. For the [nerves] growing into the liver at the porta are so small that they appear to be woven only into its membrane. And indeed one might be in doubt in the same way about the spleen and kidneys, and still more in the lung; and perhaps, if there is a sensation of weight in these viscera, it might be said to belong not to the viscera themselves but to the coats and membranes enclosing them, especially in the case of the lung and liver, which are suspended and hang, and are not firmly fixed. For patients often clearly feel a certain tension up by the collarbone, as with swellings in the liver, and the organ itself being heavy; and lucky is the person who has not felt this in his whole life, so constantly does it happen to everyone. Hippocrates too says somewhere, 'heavy pain into the kidney', just as weight also arises in the lung; and this has been said by nearly all doctors, whenever the organ is seized by inflammation. But most doctors, having investigated none of these things, and some not even [knowing] that fullness can sometimes be throughout the whole animal, but can also occur in any single part or several, pronounce rashly about fullness. But if you like, let us leave all these difficulties for the present and exercise ourselves on the easier matters.

It seems to me easier to start again from heaviness, for this appears to be the clearest sign of fullness relative to the sensitive faculty. Is it true, then, to declare that heaviness follows fullness of necessity, or that heaviness of necessity precedes fullness? For it is certainly not the same thing for heaviness to follow in the argument or to precede. It is true that whoever has a fullness of certain fluids in the body has a sensation of heaviness, evidently in those parts in which the fullness is, provided they are sensitive. But it is not true that where there is heaviness in some part, there is a fullness of humours in it. For it is possible for the faculty, when it is weak, to be weighed down by the solid parts, as in paralyses. For when the whole limb is moved by the muscles, and the muscles become too weak to move and carry it, a sensation of heaviness arises in those who are paralysed. For what is weak does not seem heavy to itself, such as the muscle, or the nerve, or in general whatever body it is that first moves the parts; rather, this affection called heaviness naturally arises in some things from something else. The nerve itself, or the tendon, or the muscle, or whatever it is that moves us, can become less toned and weaker than it was, but to weigh down itself is among the impossibilities. When it becomes better toned, then, it will make its activities stronger than before, and when less toned, weaker. For example, the muscle, if indeed it is this that moves the leg, will when healthy pull vigorously that part of the limb into which it is inserted, and when in excellent condition, most vigorously; when diseased, weakly; and when its faculty is enfeebled, faintly. But if it is not the muscle but the nerve that moves the muscle itself, then again the health and disease, the good condition and weakness, of that [nerve] will produce in the limb the effects which the muscle was said to produce. And likewise, if the pneuma is the first of the things that move the leg, these things will be said of it. Come then, for clarity's sake let this be laid down by us: that the muscle is moved by the pneuma carried through the nerves, and by the muscle first the shin, into which the muscle is inserted, and then through it the knee joint, onto which the whole leg is attached. For on these hypotheses one could truly say that the muscle itself becomes a weight to the weak pneuma, and with it the whole limb, for example the shin. But if we suppose that the nerve is moved by the pneuma, and the muscle by the nerve, and then again the shin by the muscle, the weak pneuma will be weighed down by all of the things mentioned. So it is already clear here too that it is not possible to recognise what first weighs down and what is weighed down without first knowing what first moves each of the parts in us. But this too we shall examine more precisely later; let the matter under discussion be completed. For clarity's sake the whole exposition will proceed by hypothesis. Let it be supposed, then, that the muscle is the first mover both of itself and of the bone of the shin. To itself, then, it is never heavy, not even when it is most lacking in tone, but the shin weighs it down; whether only when it sets out to move, or even when it is at rest, is [a matter] for another inquiry, and no small one, which we have determined in the work on the movement of muscles; without this inquiry it is not possible to recognise precisely either the condition or the affected place from the sensations of heaviness. For instance, in some people either one limb or the whole body feels heavy when they choose to move, but when they are at rest no sensation of heaviness arises; while some say they feel heavy even before moving. What the condition is in each of these, then, is impossible to know before discovering the moving and the moved bodies throughout the whole leg. For if the fibres of the nerves in the muscle are the first things moved, and along with them in it are moved the membranous kind, the venous and the arterial, and also the ligaments, then a sensation of heaviness will arise in it both through these and through all the other things throughout the whole limb. We shall examine and determine when the heaviness will occur while the limb is active and moving, and when while it is at rest. But if the ligamentous kind in it is also moved together with the fleshy, for these are the proper substance of the muscle, the sensation of heaviness could never arise through any of these; it will arise either from the veins, or from the arteries, or from the fat, or from the bones, or from some of these, or from all. And it is clear that if we should ever omit in such divisions the 'from some, or from all', those reading the book must understand it in addition, knowing that in all such statements the conjunctions are not exclusively disjunctive but quasi-disjunctive. From what has been said, then, it is quite clear that whoever wishes to be able to diagnose a plethoric part must have knowledge of the faculties that govern us, and of the anatomy and nature of all the parts of the animal precisely; for starting from this he might perhaps one day discover the signs of a plethoric part.

But if someone does not care for the truth, but wishes to deceive those around him into thinking he knows something clever, it is easy for him, if nothing else, at least to learn what Erasistratus [says] in the first book of his Hygiene; for elsewhere he did not even attempt to state signs of fullness. Let us attend, then, to his words, first those in which he says what the origin of plethora is (for so he himself names fullness in the veins), and then next those in which he sets out the signs for diagnosis. His account of the origin is as follows. 'When the nourishment distributed is neither digested, nor worked off as is customary for each person, nor excreted in some other way, the vessels must necessarily be filled, while digestion and distribution perform their respective activities. And when the nourishment already present in the vessels is in no way consumed, and that from what is taken in is added, the vessels in the body are stretched still further. And when the vessels no longer admit any more packing, and other nourishment is brought on from the belly, what is present takes a rush into the adjacent vessels of the pneuma.' From this, then, it is clear that he is discussing fullness in respect of the contents, and also from his calling it specifically plethora; for this affection alone is named plethora, not the other, which is judged relative to the faculty. A little further on, going through its diagnosis, he writes the following: 'One must, then, as has been said, try to diagnose the condition of plethora. At its beginning, when the vessels are moderately filled, [people] appear better toned and stronger than themselves, beyond what is customary; but when the filling goes further, the arms, the shins and the hands become filled up, as in those who come into distension after exercise; and when the plethora advances far, they have an ulcerous feeling and are slower and move with more difficulty, and the whole surface of the body is tense, as when weariness appears. Such a condition is already close to disease, unless someone resolves it very skilfully and intelligently.' In this Erasistratus has confused the signs of fullnesses of different kinds, besides adding to them some that are not necessary. One may examine his account from the beginning. For in 'at its beginning, when the vessels are moderately filled, [people] appear better toned and stronger than themselves, beyond what is customary', the statement has a necessary consequence in neither direction, neither from the condition to its signs nor from the signs to the condition. For it is neither necessary that, when the vessels are moderately filled, people appear better toned and stronger than themselves, nor that, when they appear so, the vessels have been moderately filled. For with moderate fillings of these it is possible that some people sometimes become even less toned, or change in no noticeable way in either direction, neither towards strength nor towards weakness; and if they become stronger than before, it is possible that in them the quantity of humours has not only increased along with the faculty, but has sometimes even diminished, and sometimes kept its original quantity. For on either hypothesis there may be three consequences of what was stated first: of the humours having increased, good tone and lack of tone compared with the previous state, and also the faculty's remaining within the same bounds; of [a person's] having become better toned, the [humours'] having increased, having diminished, and being in due proportion. Let it be understood in the same way in the present discussion whether I say humours or blood; for a distinction will be made about them as the discussion proceeds. Erasistratus, then, made a bare pronouncement, adding no demonstration to what he said; but we, not barely, but confirming each of the things we have just said with necessary demonstrations, shall here again make our start from Erasistratus' own words: 'they appear', he says, 'better toned and stronger'. Does 'better toned' signify something other than 'stronger', and has he taught us two signs of moderate fullness, or did he state two names but one sign? I find no difference in what is signified, neither in genus nor in species nor in degree, but I think the same thing is signified by each. But if you like, suppose that one indicates an intensification and increase over the other, whether 'stronger' over 'better toned' or 'better toned' over 'stronger'; still, what is signified by both is in any case of the same species. And where there is increase while the species remains, there is no teaching of two things signified. It is quite clear that Erasistratus makes no mention at all of the other kind of fullness, which is relative to the faculty, neither in this book nor in his work on fevers. For according to him plethora is the cause of transfusion, upon which inflammations form and fever follows; and he clearly showed the origin of plethora in the passage quoted above, in which he says that the vessels in the body are packed and stretched to the utmost. For he himself used these words, just as also [he said] that because they can no longer admit any more packing, transfusion of the surplus into the arteries occurs, the excess in the veins taking its rush there. Something has been omitted here too, then, in the division. For he ought not to have said so simply that when the veins no longer admit more packing, their contents rush into the vessels of the pneuma; it would have been much better to say that one of two things follows the aforesaid filling of the veins: either a rupture of its coat or a transfusion of the blood into the vessels of the pneuma. To think that the blood is of necessity transfused because it is not contained by the veins is the mark of one who has entirely forgotten that a rupture of a vessel sometimes occurs through fullness, to pass over the opening of mouths without transfusion that clearly often occurs into perceptible cavities of the intestines, stomach, gullet, throat and mouth. But deficiency in the division of arguments is customary for Erasistratus not only in this, but in nearly all his other treatises as well.

Let us examine again, then, what was said, whatever its nature may be. 'When the vessels are moderately filled, people appear to have better tone than before.' Is this so, Erasistratus, even if the strength of the body does not increase together with the quantity of the blood, or [only] when that strength also increases together with it? For my part I say that it is most necessary, for the good tone of the activity, that the strength of the faculty should also increase. And so, if you believe that the activities of the faculty become stronger through the increase of the blood alone, you would seem to be overturning the faculties even more than Asclepiades does. For not even he says quite so simply that whoever has more blood is in every case of better tone, and whoever has less is of necessity of poorer tone; rather you will find him stating certain qualifications that agree with what is observed, even though he believes that there is no faculty in us, neither psychic nor vital. For some people are seen to have become, at times, both fuller of blood and stronger than they were, and others both stronger and less full of blood; so that, since strength is neither necessarily increased by the quantity of the blood nor diminished by its reduction, we must consider that this too was said by Erasistratus rather carelessly. For if anyone had reminded him of what I have now gone through, he would not have denied that good tone of the activities follows not increase of the blood but strength of the faculty. Let us now, then, make his statement more complete, adding what is missing to what he said deficiently. It will be like this: when the blood increases together with the faculty, the good tone must also increase. And yet, even if we say this, we shall say something true, but we shall gain nothing more from it for the matter in hand. For the statement that in those in whom both have increased together, the blood and the faculty, the good tone has also increased, will be true; but the statement that in those in whom strength has increased, both have of necessity increased, is false. For the faculty does not of necessity increase together with an increase of the blood, but it is possible sometimes for the faculty alone [to increase]. At any rate the truly good trainer, if he takes on someone who through lack of exercise has accumulated much phlegmatic blood but is rather weak in faculty, will in a short time return him stronger, not fuller of blood, than when he took him on. So just as it is not necessary that those who have become of better tone in their activities than they were should have had their humours increased, so it is necessary that those who have become of better tone in their activities than they were should have had their faculty become stronger. And not only, starting from the good tone, will you necessarily proceed to the strength of the faculty, but also from the faculty to the good tone; for the man strong in faculty is of better tone in his activities. So they follow reciprocally upon each other: good tone in the activities upon strength of the faculty, and strength in the faculty upon good tone of the activities; for whichever of them you suppose to be present, the other is in every case present with it. But from more blood the inference is not necessary. For neither, if this is more than before, is the man of necessity of better tone, nor, if less, of poorer tone, just as neither, when it is equal, is he in the same state of faculty. So from what has been said it is clear that good tone of the activities is a sign both proper to and inseparable from the faculty's being strong, but of the increase of the blood it is neither proper nor inseparable. What Erasistratus said next is not proper to plethora, but it is inseparable from it. He calls it 'being overfilled', but it might more clearly be called 'being stretched'. Indeed the more precise trainers, calling one kind of fatigue ulcerous, another tensive, another inflammatory, indicate nothing other than the limbs' being overfilled in tensive fatigue. For they say that any part whatever is overfilled beyond its normal state whenever they perceive some tension in it. Now they perceive tension in inflammation too, but with that there is present, either always or for the most part, the unnatural throbbing, which someone expressing it more clearly will call a throbbing pain; but in those to whom nothing else has happened except being stretched, the stretched part is neither inflamed nor of necessity plethoric, but one of two things: either fatigued or plethoric. But if it is fatigued, it has been so affected after more than usual exertion; and if the man has not exerted himself at all, the part does not become fatigued through fatigue but in some other way; so it is true to say that, since there is a sensation of tension without having exercised, there is in every case plethora. And when we put it like this, the sign becomes both inseparable and proper, each of them necessarily following the other: for tension without exercise follows plethora, since it is an inseparable sign of it, as being produced by plethora as its cause; while an increase of the blood only to such a degree that it does not yet distend the veins is not yet plethora. Why then did Erasistratus mention in his statement arms and legs and hands? For such tension also arises in the neck and the back and the loins and in the chest and the lower belly. And just as Erasistratus mentioned the limbs superfluously, in the same way, and even more so, [he mentioned] the ulcerous sensation; for this is not a sign of plethora, but arises from biting humours, such as [occurs] in ulcerated parts, either when something touches them, or when serous fluid irritates them, or a drug bites them, or it arises even in movements alone. For just as tension belongs properly to a quantity of humours stretching what contains them, so the ulcerous sensation follows a biting quality; and for this reason it sometimes arises in many people even throughout the whole body, when they not only do not have plethora, but do not even have the right amount of blood.

And if this is so, as indeed it is, it is now time to make a distinction about one of the things we put off earlier, since up to this point we were examining the signs written down by Erasistratus. For as to fullness, whether it be understood relative to the faculty or relative to the space of the containing [vessels], it would surely have been better to determine whether it naturally arises in blood alone, or in all the other humours as well; but this too has been left undetermined by them. Since, then, not only these affections take hold of the humours, deficiency and fullness, but also an abnormal quality, I have asked all the physicians, both those who understand fullness relative to the faculty and those who understand it relative to the increase of the fluids, whether, when the blood alone has increased so much that it is not contained, the veins will come to be stretched; but if either phlegm into any other part, or into the veins themselves, or, together with this or apart from it, some bile, or serous fluid, or flatulent pneuma should collect in such a quantity that it can no longer be held by what contains it, will it not be necessary in this case too for the animal to perceive tension? If the stretched part is sensitive, it is necessary, upon anything that distends and is not contained, that the sensation of tension should arise in the animal, and that the affection itself, the so-called tension, should take hold of the parts; and as this increases further, it is necessary that the stretched [thing] should also burst. To me this seems to agree with what is clearly observed. For not only sinews or ropes are seen to burst from the violence of the tension, but often also jars, from must that has turned to wind. Recently, at any rate, a tin vessel was so blown out by the drug made from vipers contained in it that the skin placed around it and the cord with which it was tied burst, and the lid bulged. And indeed I think that all who take care to follow and examine what is seen day by day in the sick know that some people are at times seized by the greatest pains from flatulent pneuma trapped in certain parts of the animal, and that this usually happens most of all in the colon. It is better, then, to hold that the parts are brought into a tensive condition by every fluid and pneumatic substance, than that such an affection follows only blood, of the humours, when it increases. Let us pass over again, then, to those who believe that fullness always arises relative to the faculty, and let us ask them too one of the most obvious questions, proposing some such supposition as this by way of example. Let two men carry, placing them on their shoulders, the one a log, or a stone, or some very heavy load, the other a very few, very sharp thorns. Then let us ask, at such a sight, those who always understand fullness relative to the faculty whether they also call the few thorns a load, or whether being distressed by each of the things carried is a symptom common to the men, while the kind of distress differs very greatly: for to the one it has befallen to be weighed down without being pricked, to the other to be pricked without being weighed down. And in general, if someone calls being pricked, or bitten, or distressed in any way whatever a load and fullness, he will one day be compelled to call even a single thorn or a very fine needle a load; and what could be more ridiculous than that? These things, then, are absurd and contrary to the common notions of all men. And our purpose is not to overturn the common notions, but to preserve them. So we consider what weighs down to be much, and what bites, or pricks, or however one wishes to name it, to be distressing. And indeed that many of the humours are biting, some having their origin in ourselves, others being brought to us from outside, is quite plain to everyone. There are four differences among them, by more and less: for those that bite moderately are itch-producing, like the squill; those that bite more violently are biting, like the onion; for if our body should keep company longer with a body of such a nature, it will be ulcerated; and those that are still more acrid than this, especially when applied to ulcerated [parts], produce shivering. And when shivering is extended and increased, the symptom is called rigor. And by the same analogy biting humours arise in us in four kinds: for of them those that scratch moderately are itch-producing, those more biting than these produce an ulcerous sensation, those that bite more than these shivering, and those that are severely biting rigor. These things have been discussed in many treatises, but for one who wants to get a survey of them, what is said in the second book of The Causes of Symptoms and in the fourth of On Matters of Health is sufficient; and if one should also read through the book On the Faculty of Drugs and the treatise that precedes it, On Mixtures, he would in this way be persuaded more scientifically about the nature of biting things. But most physicians are in a condition like that described by Hippocrates concerning those who do not do what they are ordered for fractures or some such affections; for they too, although they wish to become healthy, do not endure the toil of the treatment, just as these do not endure the toil of learning. But neither is it possible to become healthy all at once, attaining the end by merely wishing it, nor for these to become scientific without going through the whole road that I have just indicated. For they will know, if they wish, that the ulcerous sensation of the whole body, both that which arises from rather much unaccustomed exercise and that which comes on suddenly without exercise, is the offspring of a biting humour. And for this reason the trainers treat those who have exercised rather much with more oil and gentle rubbing and baths of hot fresh water, exactly well tempered, so that the biting humours may be dispersed, as many as were generated, in those who exercised too immoderately, by the melting of fat and soft flesh, or through the humours themselves in the body having been strongly heated. If, then, someone should endure to learn thoroughly the demonstrations of these things, he alone would be firmly persuaded that the ulcerous condition arises from biting humours, the condition of heaviness from humours that are much relative to the faculty, and that of tension from humours that are much as well, but relative to the space containing them, not to the faculty of the (containing) bodies. Erasistratus, in the first book of On Matters of Health, when going through the generation of plethora itself, teaches most clearly the third of the conditions mentioned; but next, turning to the signs, he wrote those of this one no more than those of the others. For tension, which he named being overfilled, belongs to this alone; but the sensation's becoming ulcerous is a sign proper neither to the aforesaid fullness nor to that relative to the faculty; and much less so is people's being made heavier and harder to move; for this in fact is proper to fullness relative to the faculty. He came close, then, to writing down for us the whole concurrence of the Empiricists; indeed he also wrote part of the so-called three-time semeiosis, which the followers of Herophilus introduced in the same way as the Empiricists, in saying thus: 'For when the nourishment distributed is neither digested nor worked off as is customary for each person, nor excreted in some other way'. For it made no difference whether to say this or, as they say, an idle life and retention of customary excretions. For he indicated the previous idle life by saying 'nor worked off as is customary for each person', and the retention of excretions by adding 'nor excreted in some other way', (the indication of fullness by time) taking from the past time the idle life together with the retention of excretions; from the present time the being overfilled and the ulcerous condition, reluctance towards movement, heaviness of the whole body, and all the other such things they add; and from the future, that those in this state benefit well when evacuated, which Erasistratus has left out. For this is a testimony to correct diagnosis and treatment together; but it would be no part of diagnosis, or, as they call it, semeiosis, if indeed we want to use semeiosis to identify conditions in order to find the appropriate treatment. So if it were possible to treat appropriately starting from something else, semeiosis would be superfluous. And in mentioning the present time he has left out redness and distension of the vessels, which almost all the Empiricists add as well, and not a few of the Dogmatists, as also some other things, as has been said. And yet for those who suppose the generation of plethora to be in blood alone, redness and distension of the vessels are not badly added to the diagnosis; and still more so, since to say that the arms and hands and legs are overfilled he will assign, following his own hypotheses, no more to fullness in the flesh and whole muscles than to that of the veins. But even so it was necessary to make a twofold diagnosis, one of [the fullness of] these perceptible veins, which all of us men see, and another of that which he alone beheld. I think, then, that it has now become quite plain, to those at least who pay attention, that diagnosing fullness is no small matter. And where it is not easy to diagnose even in theory, but entirely baffling, it would hardly be achieved spontaneously in practice by those who have neither considered anything about it beforehand nor discovered it.

Let us, then, begin our account of fullness again from the Empiricists, since they seem to escape the difficulties mentioned quite safely, admitting that they themselves know nothing at all about the essence of fullness, but saying that in a certain kind of concurrence the removal of blood has been observed to be beneficial, which concurrence they name plethoric. For by gathering into one everything that has been said by each of the Dogmatists, they think that by this means they escape the difficulties of those men, but they are refuted far more than they, if one pays attention to what they say; and it is better to go through all of it again from the beginning. Let it be supposed, then, that in the past time the diet was the customary one, of the usual foods from the beginning, and with some of them taken to satiety more than before, together with a retention of excretion, and the whole way of life idle; and in the present time tension of the whole body, or of some parts, reluctance to move, lack of tone in the activities, and a sensation of heaviness and of an ulcerous condition, together with swelling of the veins; and let redness also be added, if you like, since some mention this as well, and indeed also swelling of the whole body, and an uneven and fatigue-like condition; for there are those who add these too. We shall ask them, then, what I asked my Empiricist teacher when I was a youth, when he first taught me these things: must all the things mentioned come together for, as they themselves say, the recollection of evacuation, or if they see even one of them, will they let blood at once? To the first question he readily answered me, saying that all must come together; for such is the nature of the concurrence, a collection of all the things that make it up. But when I first reminded him of two men whom he himself had recently ordered to be bled, one suffering severely from ophthalmia, the other who had fallen from his carriage and then become entangled in the reins and been dragged a long way, so that some parts were bruised; and after this, when he fell silent, I recalled yet another, whom he bled while he had a moderate fever but could not bear the pain in his head; and another with pleurisy, who did not have the whole concurrence mentioned either; he was reduced to the greatest perplexity. And so I went on to describe to him at greater length some other similar cases as well, and also reminded him about those mentioned, that he had bled them although they were so far from having the whole concurrence that I said I could not recall even two of these things being present in the men. For the one who fell from the carriage, who exercised every day, was adequately evacuated by all his customary excretions, ate moderately, spent almost the whole day with us, and seemed neither to him nor to anyone else to need evacuation, he judged worthy of venesection when, having been thrown down, he bruised some parts, though he had acquired neither any redness, nor swelling of the vessels, nor anything else of what belongs to the concurrence, but only had pain in the bruised parts. In the same way too the one with ophthalmia and the one with the headache, who had none at all of the things mentioned in the plethoric concurrence; and I know of many others bled by us who either had nothing at all of the plethoric concurrence, or at any rate not all together the things spoken of by us. For now, I said, as I call to mind those whom I saw bled by you, I cannot find one among them who had the whole concurrence of such symptoms; but one man was bled because he was fatigued, having nothing else; another because he was in a high fever, or had pain in the eyes or the head, or had his haemorrhoids stopped, or a woman her menses, but not all the things which the plethoric concurrence requires to come together. If, then, you call all the conditions in which venesection has been observed to be beneficial plethoric, it is time for us to call ophthalmia, pleurisy, severe pain, a fall from a carriage, and countless other things plethoric concurrences; but if none of these is included in the plethoric concurrence, and the collection of symptoms mentioned earlier is named the plethoric concurrence, no one should be bled before he has all of them. How he met me on these points, and answered nothing fitting, would be a task of long leisure, not a task proper to what is now before us; and since I do not now have leisure for idle talk, I decided not [to do so] now, but in my account of venesection I have chosen to set out all the aims of this remedy, which no one has written down accurately and with distinctions either.

Leaving aside, then, for the present the dispute with the Empiricists, I return again to the Rationalists, examining each of the symptoms they have written down. For some of them belong to fullness relative to the faculty, some to fullness in respect of the contents, some are signs not of fullness simply but of a particular kind of fullness, and some of no fullness at all, but either of bad humours and corruption, or of a weak faculty, or of a swelling of the solid bodies. That this is so, you will learn if you pay attention to what is about to be said. The tensive condition, then, when it occurs without exercise, indicates in every case that much substance is contained in a sensitive body, but it does not further indicate what the substance is, or its kind, at least by this alone, the being stretched, which is common to every substance, thin and thick and intermediate in consistency, and pneumatic, and further hot and cold, or intermediate; rather it needs some other distinguishing marks for determining this. Lack of tone in the activities shows that the faculty is weaker, by holding back what moves, as in a weak movement of the hands; for it follows many states. For if in someone the fleshy and fatty kind should increase, while the faculty remains within the same limits, the movements must become less vigorous, since what moves stays equal while what is moved has increased; or if some one of the humours, or even all of them together, should become excessive, without the faculty increasing along with them, then too the activities must become less vigorous; or if both should increase together, the so-called parenchymata and the fluids, but the faculty does not increase with them, or if, these remaining as they were, the faculty becomes weaker. It could also happen sometimes that both come together, so that the faculty becomes weaker and the humours together with the parenchymata are either more or less, or whichever one of them; the activities become less vigorous for these reasons too, whether each of them occurs singly, or two, or more, or all together. For to think that a less vigorous movement could ever be produced by the good nourishment of the solid bodies belongs to men who do not know that the faculties pervade the solid bodies throughout, but who make the arteries and the nerves like pipes or channels for pneuma. You will know the badness of this opinion from many other [works], but not least from two treatises of ours, the one On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato and the one On the Natural Faculties. Good nourishment of the solid bodies, then, is proper to good condition, while increase of the flesh is proper to good flesh and to excess of flesh. For the most part, then, the fat increases in proportion, more [than the flesh], but sometimes in fat [people] the flesh more, or the fat alone. These matters have been discussed in the commentaries On Temperaments. And just as in flesh one thing is good flesh and another excess of flesh, in the same way in blood one thing is a sort of good blood, the other excess of blood. Now it is not unclear that the state of good blood is exactly according to nature in both quality and quantity; while that of excess of blood is blameless in quality, but not blameless in quantity, but in every case more, either than what was natural from birth, or than what is relative to the faculty. For it is possible sometimes for both to increase together, beyond the nature from birth, the strength of the faculty and the quantity of the blood, as in athletic good condition; for in these the fluids and the fleshy parts and the faculty increase together in proportion to one another. And so it is now quite plain that those who called swelling of the body one of the plethoric signs do not speak truly either; for swelling of the veins would be a plethoric sign, but swelling of flesh and fat would be a fullness of those things themselves, not, however, that which we are now seeking, which is also called plethora. For having proposed to speak about this fullness, which evidently indicates evacuation, some of them went astray so far, [misled by] what is at times indicated by homonymies, as to be carried off to the fullness of flesh and fat. So bad a mark of fullness, then, is swelling of the body; for it would indicate the filling of those very veins that we see, but not necessarily of those in the depth; rather it is possible sometimes that, while the outer veins are distended, the inner ones are not distended in the same way; for example, when cold has taken hold, the blood is driven into the depth, and the outer [veins] are so drained of blood that they do not even appear; and again when there is warmth, or after bathing, the blood is carried to the skin and the outer parts of the body, leaving the depth; and if there is also a burning fever, then too the blood must be heated by the body, boiling as it is, and become vaporous and expand. So swelling of the veins is not an inseparable mark of a quantity of humours, but first the body must be in such a state that neither the inner parts exceed the outer in heat nor these the inner; and second, that there is no immoderate heat in the whole animal. With these distinctions made beforehand, swelling of the veins might be a sign of the fullness now called sanguine, [so called] by predominance; for it is impossible that blood so pure should ever be contained in the veins that nothing of bile, or phlegm, or serous fluid is carried along with it, which is why earlier too I asked that it be understood in the same way whether I said that the humours were in excess or the blood. For since blood unmixed and pure of the other fluids is never contained in the veins (this has been shown by us elsewhere), but mixed blood, mixed not at random but with the others mingled with it in a certain proportion in animals in a natural state, it will make no difference whether we call it humours or blood. For when all increase together, in the natural proportion, with the blood that predominates, the name humours signifies the same thing, and it makes no difference whether we say the humours or the blood have increased, since the statement that says humours indicates just this, that there is an excess while the original proportion is wholly kept. Let this, then, be distinguished thus by us, and let us go back again to the matter in hand. Swelling of the veins, if it has arisen neither through predominance of the external state nor through diffusion and boiling, indicates that the fullness is sanguine. But such a part must also not be positioned hanging downward, or have been moved recently more than the others; therefore one might, gathering all the particular distinctions in one statement, say that swelling of the veins indicates a quantity of blood when all the parts have the same state together with moderate warmth; since if all were in the same condition but there were immoderate heat, there arises in this case a diffusion of the humours that raises the veins into swelling, which indicates a fullness not sanguine but pneumatic; for the humours become pneumatic when heated. Therefore those too who declared that swelling of the veins signifies fullness will seem to have spoken correctly, if one understands in the statement 'in those veins', in which this happens to occur; for the substance that has produced the swelling in the veins is necessarily more than before, but it is not yet clear what kind the fullness is; for unnatural swelling is common to every abundant substance, whether it is pure blood, or bilious, or serous, or phlegmatic, or pneumatic. Just as this is common to every kind of fullness, so too is the tension of the veins; for this too follows the quantity of the fullness, not its difference in kind. So the swelling and the tensive sensation will no more indicate a fullness of humours than of pneuma. If, then, someone were to declare something like this: 'in tensive sensations there is necessarily fullness', he will speak truly; and indeed if he were to say this: 'fullness in sensitive parts brings on a certain condition', he too will speak truly; but if someone, leaving aside the generic name 'fullness' or 'the humours', were to substitute 'blood' in the statement, he will not necessarily speak truly, for the reasons we have given. That the swelling of the veins and the tensive condition mark a difference not of fullness simply, but of the greater and lesser degree within it, is clear from this. No part feels pain when it is filled unless violent tension has first arisen in it; but if it is raised into swelling, yet not yet violently, it is not yet stretched; therefore of swellings, the one with tension will indicate more fullness, and the one without it, less. How, then, is it that sometimes no swelling at all appears in the veins, yet the tensive sensation is strong? For surely the condition of being stretched ought to be joined with the greatest swellings. Either because sometimes the swelling distends only the veins in the depths, or, if within the relative fullness of which we are now speaking there is both the [fullness] relative to the width of the vessels, which we call fullness while they are not yet stretched, and that relative to the tension of the coat, then clearly the formation of the swelling of the veins advances as the blood increases to a quantity beyond the natural proportion of each, so that 'much' is said relative to that; but the stretching of the coat indicates excess beyond the proportion relative to the coat itself. For it is not natural for this either to be stretched. Each, then, is 'much': the blood relative to the natural proportion, and relative to the tension of the coat. Erasistratus mentioned both, not articulately, nor as clearly as I do now, yet so as to show that the nature of the matter is twofold. For in saying, 'At first, then, when the vessels are moderately filled, they appear of better tone and stronger than themselves, contrary to what is usual', he indicated the disproportion of the blood beyond what is natural for each; and in what he says next, adding, 'But as they come to a greater degree of filling, the arms and hands and shins become overfilled', [he indicated] that relative to the coats containing the blood; so that there are two limits of the increase of blood beyond the natural: one in which the coats of the veins are filled and raised into swelling beyond what is natural for each, and the other in which, in addition to this, they happen to be stretched, neither of these being seen in the fullness relative to the faculty. About these things, then, this too is enough.

Redness, which they also mention, is a sign not of fullness simply but of sanguine fullness. It too will need the same distinctions as the swelling; for if [it arises] through some external cause, such as sun, or a bath, or exercise, or walking, or, to speak simply, warmth, and likewise anger, shame and all such things; and acute fevers too are of this kind. When, then, the condition of the whole body is uniform and none of the things I have mentioned is present, then redness would be a sign of sanguine fullness throughout the whole animal; if not, then at least in that part in which it appears; for such a colour also accompanies inflammations, whether they form in the muscles or in the skin, these being plethoric diseases. But inflammations have been discussed sufficiently in another writing, in which we examined unnatural swellings, showing that all of them arise from a fullness of fluids descending now on one part, now on another; now, however, the account is not about these, but, as was said before, about that fullness which is called plethora, when an excess of humours forms in the whole body. We do not say that fullness forms in the whole body in such a way that both kinds of bodies are harmed, that of the vessels and that of the flesh; for it is possible at times for only one of the two [to be affected], provided that whichever part is seized, this has occurred not in one or two parts but either throughout the whole animal or in the most numerous and most important parts. And so, to discover of what kind the swelling is requires a man well trained in diagnosis. In the fleshy kind, at any rate, the swelling of the flesh itself is one thing, and that of the fluids another, as when the flesh, like some wool or sponge, is filled with superfluous moisture; but such a fullness in the flesh is analogous to the one called 'in the contents' in the case of the vessels, and the other fullness to that relative to the faculty, or with heaviness; we remembering that it made no difference whether one speaks of composite flesh or of muscles, and that whenever the account concerns fullness in the flesh, one must understand the muscles, not that simple flesh which some call parenchyma. In the arteries and the veins, however, the fullness relative to the faculty is not similarly perceptible to the patients themselves; but only to those who are by nature most sensitive does a faint and deep heaviness show itself in the body; therefore one must seek other, clearer signs of such fullness. Since most physicians have been careless about this, some not examining it at all and some deficiently, no sign has been found more reliable than the motion of the arteries, which we have explained sufficiently in our treatises on the pulse. For in most cases the veins enter a state of plethora together with the arteries, because of the confluence of the vessels, which we have often demonstrated elsewhere; but sometimes, when viscous or thick humours have collected in the veins, their passage into the arteries does not happen easily, though such a thing is rare; for unless the humours are extremely thick or viscous, they will certainly flow across. In such conditions, then, no clear sign of the fullness collected in the veins can be taken from the motion of the arteries, however much Nicarchus and Praxagoras may think so, though they do not let the arteries share in blood; in the other conditions of plethora, however, one should trust the signs from the pulses, which have been stated in the treatise proper to them, and distinguish the kinds of fullness, when it is spread uniformly through the whole body, as follows. The fullness of blood is very red, that of yellow bile pale-yellowish, and it turns whiter than natural when phlegm predominates, just as it turns darker if black bile does. In each of the cases mentioned the blood too must have increased together; for if ever the bile called pale and yellow abounds alone, as in the jaundiced, such an affection is no longer fullness, nor a plethoric condition, but bad humour. The same holds for black bile and phlegm. When, as was said before, there is either heaviness or swelling beyond the natural, such a condition has been called plethoric, and one must recognise the kind of the predominating humour from the colour. Bile alone can produce neither of the symptoms inseparable from fullness, neither the swelling nor the heaviness; for some other affection will arise from it before it increases to that extent. Phlegm alone, if any, and not all of it simply, but that in the dropsies called leucophlegmatic, will be able to abound in the whole body. It is clear that the humour called raw must also be placed, in the present account at least, as one of the kinds of phlegm, since if we set it down as different from that, we must add to the differences of fullness we have just named the one from such a humour too; this humour is thicker than other phlegm and less pneumatic, such as settles in the urine, especially of those who from gluttony have a copious sediment resembling bean soup; and indeed such a humour has often passed downward all at once in those bodies which abstained from exercise but used very many foods, and baths after meals; but with this humour too, as with phlegm, a white pallor coexists throughout the whole body. Of the other kinds of phlegm, one is sweet, one sour, one salty; and people become sleepy with the sweet, hungry when the sour abounds, just as they become thirsty when the salty predominates; and without appetite with the raw [humour] mentioned before. As for sleep, with the other phlegms mentioned before it is a little more than natural; but the raw humour, like sweet phlegm, clearly makes people sleepy; for it has been shown elsewhere that when the sensitive principle is moistened and cooled, the comatose condition follows, just as sleeplessness does when it is dried and heated. That is why those suffering from bile are all sleepless, with either bile; but with black bile there is in particular gloominess and despondency without reason. If the humours mentioned do not abound in the whole body but collect in some one part, they produce unnatural swellings in the bodies themselves, about which it is shown elsewhere. And the very symptoms of them now mentioned, except for the pallor, belong to [humours] that have seized the brain and the stomach; for sleeplessness and sleep come about through the brain, and appetites and loss of appetite through the stomach, as it is disposed now one way, now another. It is clear that by 'stomach' the mouth of the belly is now meant, in which the phlegm that has collected, as was said a little before, produced the appetites; while of the bilious [humours], with yellow bile people will be thirsty and nauseated, and their mouth is bitter; with black bile they are despondent, gloomy, fearful, without thirst and full of saliva, and not all of them are off their food, but some of them are. Those are quite hungry whose black bile has the sour quality predominating; and this happens when it has become more malignant. So long as it is only like a sediment of blood, and not yet sharply sour, it is perhaps better (so long as it is called melancholic humour) not yet to call such a humour black bile at all, but, as I usually do, melancholic, because it has come close to becoming black bile. But now is not the time to go through the difference among the bad humours, since I said that they are not called fullness either; our purpose was not simply to find out whatever is in excess in any way, but to examine fullness; and this is an excess of the humours throughout the whole body of the animal. So in this discourse one must not expect to hear the kinds either of local swellings or of bad humour, but [only] the case when either all [the humours] have increased in their original proportion, or one of them has gained some slight predominance. Now the blood can gain a very great predominance in plethoric conditions, but none of the other humours can; for that sort of thing is already bad humour, and is no longer called fullness or plethora. That is also why in the bad humours the pulses correspond exactly to the nature of the humours; but in the fullnesses mentioned they do not preserve the differences so clearly, because the humour in excess is always together with abundant blood; but when it prevails strongly, with yellow bile the pulses must become such as we said follow when the heart is dried and heated; with black bile, again, such as we said occur if it is cooled and dried; and by the same reasoning, if phlegm should ever overcome the others, it will produce pulses that are the offspring of a cold and moist condition. Blood that is exactly natural is followed by no alteration of the original state; but when blood moister [than normal] is in excess the pulses are also altered with it, just as if it became hotter or colder than itself. All such matters have been distinguished in the treatise on the pulses; for now it will suffice to say this much: that from idleness and a moist diet the blood may become moister than itself, through an excess of watery residues; and from anger and exercises, from exposure to heat and rubbings, from a heating drug and similar food, and from wines less diluted and older, hotter, just as through some recent chilling, colder. And if someone uses for a longer time foods drier in mixture, but having no other bad mixture, that blood would become drier. And indeed, in combination too, it will be made moister and colder, or colder and drier, hotter and moister, or hotter and drier by the causes mentioned, without any of the other humours gaining predominance. But if it should come into a bad mixture through admixture of those [humours], such a bad mixture would arise together with bad humour, the blood still being said even then to have become either hotter, or colder and moister, and so on for the other six bad mixtures, for there were eight in all, but in another way, not as when it was of such a kind alone by itself. The pulses in the eight bad mixtures will have the form that we went through in the treatise on the pulses; but whether, as has been said, it belongs to the blood alone, or is due to some admixture of a humour, must be distinguished by the accompanying colour of the whole body, and by the other symptoms concerning sleep and waking, or appetite and loss of appetite, or anything of that kind, mentioned a little before, and by the preceding diet, the exercises, and what usually befalls the patient himself, and further by the season, the region, and the natural density and rarity of the body; for it is better to take the assurance for the diagnosis from all [of these], not from one or two, knowing well that this alone in the art has the greatest share in conjecture, I mean this whole diagnostic part of the art, not only that concerning bad humour or fullness, which we now propose to distinguish; for matters concerning functions, or the causes of diseases, or cures, admit of more scientific knowledge. These very things have been discussed at greater length elsewhere, and now it will suffice, having adequately distinguished what has been added, to end the treatise somewhere about here. The account would be adequate if examined with an example. Let the man, then, be without fever, but his veins of greater bulk and his whole body redder. One must consider, then, whether any of the heating causes has come near him; for if one should appear, it is better to postpone the diagnosis until the movement from it has settled down in the whole body, because one should not bring [a person] to diagnosis while angry, or having bathed or bathing, or having exercised, or having just taken wine, or heated in any other way whatever, but when he is at rest from all external movements; for if he appears such at that time, blood is in excess in the man. Thereafter one should examine the other things, first those that have the greatest weight, then the rest in order; and it was shown [that these are] heaviness and tension, and reluctance to move, and next the features of the pulses, sleeplessness and sleep, appetites and loss of appetite, and other such things. After these, each of the preceding [causes] that produce fullness: whether some habitual excretion has been held back, whether exercise has been neglected, whether more and very nourishing food has been taken continually, whether he uses unaccustomed baths after food, and in addition to these, whether such a man is often seized by plethoric diseases. On top of all these, adding also the [indications] from the region and season, or anything else of that kind, [one should judge,] not assigning equal weight to all, just as in the other parts of the art either; for some of the signs are scientific, such as the tension, the heaviness, the bulk of the veins, the reluctance, the colour, and the movement of the pulses, all recent movements, of course, being excluded; others fall short of these, such as the holding back of excretions, an idle life, more plentiful and nourishing foods, and baths after food; yet all of them together come close to the scientific ones. Third in rank after these is whether the man is habitually seized by plethoric diseases; and next the [factors] of regions and seasons that help to bring all these about; for in winter and spring and in cold and temperate regions people accumulate fullness more, and less in hot and dry seasons and regions; and so too those dense on the surface [do so] more, and those that are rare more seldom.
